newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa edges towards abortion on demand.
newsitem.headline: South Africa edges towards abortion on demand.

text.p: South Africa's parliament on Tuesday edged towards a vote on a bill that would give the country one of the most liberal laws on abortion in the world.

Passage of the Choice on Termination of Pregnancy Bill was assured by the support of President Nelson Mandela's majority African National Congress (ANC), which has refused its members a free vote on the issue of providing state-funded abortion on demand.

Though the draft law was debated on Tuesday, the vote was postponed to Wednesday after a technical delay forced by the white-led National Party (NP), which opposes abortion, but has allowed its members to vote according to their own consciences.
The NP put forward a number of last-minute amendments that will have to be voted down by an ANC-dominated parliamentary committee before the draft law can be adopted.
The public gallery was packed by a divided crowd that jeered and cheered each speaker on the most contentious moral question yet put to South Africa's first democratic parliament.
Health Minister Nkosazana Zuma said the bill, which provides for state-funded abortion on demand up to the end of the 12th week of pregnancy, would treat women with dignity and compassion.
She said that while doctors and midwives would have to encourage consultation and counselling, neither married women nor minors would need to consult anyone before terminating a pregnancy.
The bill provides for abortion up to the end of the 20th week under conditions including rape and the likely influence of childbirth on the socio-economic circumstances of the woman.
"Just how far away are we from another Soddom and Gomorrah? Abortion on demand is simply cold-blooded murder and should not be allowed," said National Party legislator Cyril George.
ANC legislator Pregs Govender argued, however, that there was no place for an anti-abortion lobby in a country plagued by child labour, child starvation and child abuse.
"Who are we to say we care about life, that we care about children and about human suffering when United Nations figures show 84,000 children dying before the age of five in our country.
"Where was the outrage, where were the edicts from those who stand in pulpits now and hail down stones and talk of sin?" she said.

The likely passage of the bill through the National Assembly on Wednesday and through the Senate next week will end a Calvinist tradition that has allowed abortion only after rape or for women whose health is seriously at risk.
About 1,000 mainly white women have had abortions under the existing law every year, but about 400 women, mostly black, die every year as a result of botched backstreet abortions.
"Hundreds of women, more than all the members of the National Assembly, die annually from these unsafe and illegal terminations of pregnancy," said Zuma.
"This bill will save their lives by giving them a choice to terminate the pregnancy safely and in dignity."
